rv.q: Lavin wonderful in witty, touching Greenberg play.
She owns this part and claims it like nobody's business but her own.
As he approaches the second act, though, Mr. Greenberg introduces a screeching plot twist, culled from the pages of Cold War history, that upsets the play’s delicate balance.
Unfortunately, there’s almost no way to tell ahead of time when one of those daring ideas will pay off and when it will break the bank.
Based on the evidence here, it’s difficult to imagine anyone finding much emotional depth in this curdled bummer.
Lavin’s keen acerbic wit is wasted on lines like that and on a character like Anna, who is, truth to tell, a sour woman with bitter views of everyone but herself.
It’s hard to imagine an affair torrid enough to shake up a play this smug.

Linda Lavin is alternately sardonic and fragile in the New York premiere of Richard Greenberg's drama "Our Mother's Brief Affair"...The notion of "legacy" weighs heavily in the drama, which touches on themes such as the suburban dream, and the desire, when one's life is nearing its end, "to be known"...Lavin...

If Mr. Greenberg was attempting to give us something with socio-politico-historical import--like the aforementioned Other Desert Cities, for instance, or Anthony Giardina's City of Conversation--he has not convincingly done so.
A Richard Greenberg play at Manhattan Theatre Club is theatrical comfort food; this is his 11th MTC production. Somehow, Our Mother's Brief Affair got overcooked.
The play has witty lines and a few surprises, but it’s also sluggish, messy and short on plot.
OUR MOTHER'S BRIEF AFFAIR is hardly one to remember.
The cast is fine, but can only do so much with a script that is undercooked and overwritten at the same time.
In the end, however, this is a story that lacks purpose and drive.
Neither the petulant performances by Kate Arrington and Greg Keller nor the arch writing by Greenberg is compelling.
The play's switcheroo invites deep thoughts, such as, "What was that all about?"
It’s a beautiful, heart-stopping moment, but it’s not enough to save an otherwise meandering, anemic work.

cn.t: Linda Lavin delivers a standout performance in Richard Greenberg's underwhelming play, but critics find the drama unfocused, anemic, and lacking tension despite the star's witty command of another difficult Jewish mother role.
